sections.h2: Where is Ward County, North Dakota, and what is in it?
sections.html:
Ward County sits in north-central North Dakota, and its county seat and largest city is Minot. The county covers about 2,056 square miles, of which roughly 2,013 are land, according to the Census-based figures on its Wikipedia entry. It borders Renville County to the north, McHenry County to the east, McLean County to the south and Mountrail County to the west, with Burke County touching its northwest corner.

The legislature created the county on April 14, 1885 and it was organized that November 23. It carries the name of Mark Ward. The 2020 census counted 69,919 residents, which made it the fourth-most populous county in the state.

Beyond Minot, the incorporated cities are Berthold, Burlington, Carpio, Des Lacs, Donnybrook, Douglas, Kenmare, Makoti, Ryder, Sawyer and Surrey. Minot Air Force Base is a census-designated place of its own, and parts of the Des Lacs, Hiddenwood and Upper Souris National Wildlife Refuges fall inside the county line. Most of the land outside the towns is farmland.

U.S. Highways 2, 52 and 83 cross the county, along with North Dakota Highways 5, 23, 28 and 50.

sections.h2: What drives the Ward County economy, and why does it matter to a seller?
sections.html:
Minot Air Force Base is the largest single employer in Ward County. The Minot Area Chamber EDC reported in February 2026 that the base generated $956.7 million in economic impact in fiscal year 2025, with total on-base employment estimated at 6,957 jobs and more than 11,000 people living on or tied to the base when service members, family members and civilian employees are counted. Details are in the chamber's economic impact announcement.

The chamber's own description of the region also points to agriculture, with 15 commodities that rank near the top nationally, and to the energy activity of the Bakken region. The Wikipedia entry for the county notes that the area is largely devoted to agriculture.

That mix shapes how houses sell. Service members move on orders, so a seller tied to the base may need a closing date they can plan around.

sections.h2: How is a Ward County house taxed?
sections.html:
North Dakota taxes a house on a taxable value equal to 4.5 percent of its true and full value, multiplied by the combined mill levy of every local taxing district. The Office of State Tax Commissioner explains the method. A mill is one tenth of one percent, so you multiply taxable value by 0.001 and then by the total mills on your statement.

State materials define assessed value as 50 percent of market value, and a residential building is one that provides separate family living quarters for fewer than four family units. Apartment buildings with four or more units are classed as commercial.

The State Tax Commissioner works through a sample of a $275,000 home with a 250-mill levy: $12,375 of taxable value, about $12.38 per mill, and $3,095 of tax. Ward County levies will differ, and the county treasurer's statement shows the real mills. As a rough illustration only, the Census median owner-occupied value shown earlier on this page, $259,100, produces a taxable value of $11,659.50 and about $11.66 per mill before any credits.

North Dakota offers a primary residence credit, a homestead property tax credit with a renter's refund, and a disabled veteran's credit. Each has its own eligibility rules on the state tax site, and a seller who has been claiming one should note that a buyer will need to qualify on their own.

sections.h2: When are Ward County property taxes due, and what is the penalty for paying late?
sections.html:
Real estate taxes in Ward County become due on January 1 of the year after the tax year, and the first installment is delinquent after March 1. The dates come from North Dakota Century Code chapter 57-20, which the county treasurer follows.

DateWhat happens
January 1Taxes for the prior tax year become due.
February 15Last day to pay in full and take the 5 percent discount (paid or postmarked).
March 1First installment is delinquent after this date; a 3 percent penalty applies.
May 1Another 3 percent penalty is added to unpaid first-installment taxes.
July 1Another 3 percent penalty is added.
October 15Second installment is delinquent after this date, with a 6 percent penalty; unpaid first-installment taxes pick up a further 3 percent.

The 5 percent discount applies to general real estate taxes paid in full by February 15, and the treasurer applies it before any primary residence credit. It does not apply to personal property taxes or special assessment installments. If county commissioners declare an emergency from weather or another catastrophe, they may extend the discount period by 30 days.

The statute also says that failing to receive a statement does not release an owner from liability. Ward County's property tax page says the same discount rule applies to mobile homes, and the county's online payments page says statements are printed to reflect the discount when full payment arrives by February 15.

sections.h2: How do you appeal a Ward County assessment?
sections.html:
Begin with the Tax Equalization office, then go to the local board of equalization in April, then to the county board, and finally to the State Board of Equalization. The Ward County Tax Equalization office is at 225 Third St. SE, Suite 232 in Minot, 58701, and its number is 701-857-6430. County guidance says that if you do not get satisfaction from the assessor, you can take the appeal to the local board of equalization.

County pages say a township board meets the second Monday in April, and the City of Minot says its City Board of Equalization meets the second Tuesday of April on a schedule set by the county tax director. The City of Minot lists a contact at 701-857-4108 for the city board. Dates can shift, so confirm them each year.

The state-level rule matters if you want to go further. A State Board of Equalization staff report cites NDCC 57-13-04.3, which requires anyone appealing to the state board to have applied to both the local and county boards first. You can also contact the State Property Tax division at propertytax@nd.gov or 701-328-3127 to start a state appeal, where you will complete a questionnaire and submit evidence.

  • Gather recent comparable sales and any appraisal.
  • Photograph defects the assessor may not know about.
  • Bring your notice and parcel number to the April meeting.

sections.h2: What should Ward County sellers know about winter and flooding?
sections.html:
Minot's cold is severe enough to matter to a house inspection. The National Weather Service lists a record low of minus 49 degrees Fahrenheit for Minot in February, and minus 47 in January, in its North Dakota climate extremes table. Furnaces, pipes and roofs in older homes take real wear from that, and a buyer's inspector will look.

Flooding is the other part of local memory. A U.S. Geological Survey summary of the 2011 Souris River flood says more than 4,000 homes in Minot flooded and about 11,000 people were evacuated. A city program tied to a floodplain buyout process aimed to give residents whose homes were damaged or bought out access to affordable housing, according to an adaptation case study.

Fifteen years after the flood, local television reporting in June 2026 returned to the topic of costly flood insurance premiums and coming changes to FEMA maps. A seller whose house sits near the Souris River should expect questions about flood zone status and insurance cost, and a cash buyer who purchases as-is can simply price that uncertainty rather than asking you to resolve it before closing.

sections.h2: What happens to unpaid property tax if you sell a Ward County house?
sections.html:
Unpaid property tax stays attached to the property, so it is normally paid out of your sale proceeds at closing. The title company will order a tax search and ask the county treasurer for the amounts due, including any penalty that has built up since March 1 or October 15.

Because installments carry 3 percent penalties that stack on a schedule, an owner who sold in the summer after missing the March 1 date would face the first 3 percent penalty plus the May 1 and July 1 additions. Paying before the next date stops the next penalty, and asking the treasurer for a payoff figure for a specific day avoids surprises.

  • Ask the county treasurer or your title officer for a written payoff good through the closing date.
  • Check for special assessments, which are not eligible for the 5 percent discount.
  • Confirm whether any primary residence or homestead credit you used will end with the sale.

On a cash sale, the same steps apply, but there is no lender underwriting to hold up the payoff.

faqs.q: When is the Ward County property tax discount deadline?
faqs.a: February 15. Pay all of the year's real estate taxes in full on or before that date, or have the payment postmarked by then, and the county treasurer allows a 5 percent discount under NDCC 57-20-09. Ward County says its statements are printed to reflect the discount.

faqs.q: Where do I mail a Ward County property tax payment?
faqs.a: The listing we confirmed gives the address as Ward County Treasurer, PO Box 5005, Minot ND 58702. Online payment is available by credit card or e-check, so check the county's online payments page before you mail anything.

faqs.q: How do I appeal my Ward County assessment?
faqs.a: Talk to the Ward County Tax Equalization office first, then take your case to the township or city board of equalization in April, then the county board. A state appeal requires that you applied to the local and county boards first.

faqs.q: What is the penalty if I miss March 1?
faqs.a: A 3 percent penalty applies to the first installment of real estate tax after March 1. Further 3 percent penalties are added on May 1, July 1 and October 15, and the second installment carries a 6 percent penalty if it is not paid by October 15.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Ward County house that still has tax due?
faqs.a: Yes. The unpaid amount, with any penalty, is paid from the proceeds at closing. A buyer who purchases as-is for cash can close on a timeline that suits you, and the title company settles the tax with the treasurer.
